paragraphs.heading: What a whale is
paragraphs.text: Whales are a varied and widespread group of placental mammals that live fully in the sea. In everyday speech the word covers the large cetaceans, meaning every member of the infraorder Cetacea except dolphins and porpoises. In a formal, cladistic view, dolphins and porpoises can count as whales too. Whales feed, mate and give birth at sea, and they suckle and raise their young there too.

paragraphs.heading: Cousins of the hippo
paragraphs.text: Whales evolved from mammals that lived on land. Together with dolphins and porpoises they belong to the order of even-toed ungulates, and their closest living relatives outside the cetaceans are hippopotamuses, from which they split about 54 million years ago. The two groups of whales, baleen whales and toothed whales, are thought to have shared a last common ancestor around 34 million years ago.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways to eat
paragraphs.text: Baleen whales have no teeth. Instead they carry plates of baleen, fringe-like structures that let them push out huge gulps of water while keeping back the krill and plankton they eat. Their heads can make up as much as 40% of their body mass, and throat pleats let their mouths expand to take in vast amounts of water. Toothed whales instead have cone-shaped teeth for catching fish or squid, and hearing so keen that some can survive even when blind.

paragraphs.heading: Built for the sea
paragraphs.text: Whales must come up regularly to breathe air, but they can stay under for long periods; the sperm whale can last up to 90 minutes. They breathe through blowholes, which are modified nostrils on top of the head. They are warm-blooded and have blubber, a layer of fat under the skin. Streamlined bodies and two limbs shaped into flippers carry them at up to 20 knots, though seals are more flexible and agile.

paragraphs.heading: Giants and travellers
paragraphs.text: Whales range from the dwarf sperm whale, 2.6 metres and 135 kilograms, to the blue whale, 29.9 metres and 190 tonnes, the largest animal known to have lived. No toothed predator on Earth is bigger than the sperm whale. Most species prefer colder waters and migrate toward the equator to give birth, and humpbacks and blue whales can travel thousands of miles without feeding. Whales make many kinds of sounds, notably the long songs of humpbacks.

paragraphs.heading: Hunted, then protected
paragraphs.text: Whales were once hunted relentlessly for their products, but international law now protects them. North Atlantic right whales nearly went extinct in the twentieth century, dropping to a low of 450. Whales also face bycatch and marine pollution. Females mate only every two to three years and carry all the work of raising calves, and in some species mothers fast while nursing their young for one to two years. Today whale watching is a form of tourism around the world.
